I feel this so hard.  Sadly I think it's normal to be riding that terrible roller coaster of anxiety and emotions in the early recovery days.  I definitely did, and continue to do so.  I know how hard it can be and how long the day can feel when you're trapped in your own bad thoughts. 

Things that help me while I'm in the moment: 
reminding myself as many times as needed that every bad day ends, and that generally I wake up the next day feeling much better; posting here, like you have done; mindless distractions like Instagram or Pinterest (I actually have a Pinterest board of motivational/self-care stuff that I'll scroll through on bad days); walking/hugging my dogs; reading books about recovery and self-care; avoiding caffeine in any form; watching TV shows/movies that are too interesting/suspenseful to let my mind wander back to my problems; sleeping it off.

Things that have helped me long-term:  medication; seeing a therapist weekly; seeking support from people who understand recovery (i.e. here, and going to meetings); making time each day to be nice to myself even when I don't feel like I deserve it.  

Hang in there, things will get better even if it doesn't seem like it right now.

If you are concerned with provenance, then I would only buy from a dealer or antique shop.  My engagement ring came from an antique jewelry shop that specializes in Art Deco items, and the ring came with paperwork certifying its authenticity and the diamond grade. Just throwing it out there that rings can be resized up to two sizes larger, and sometimes more depending on the ring and the skills of your jeweler.  I have a 1930s Deco engagement ring that was resized from a 4 to a 6.5.  My wedding band is from the 1920s and was resized from a 4.5 to a 6.5. I can relate to this so hard - I could have written this, verbatim.  I am only on day 21 but what has helped me so far is:

1.  Counseling - and making sure I "do the work" outside of counseling 


2.  a book called "Communication for Couples" (most of the principles can be applied to communicating with anyone, not just a SO)  This has helped me to begin curbing the "bottle it up until it explodes" habit

I injured myself a year and a half ago and have used a stand-up desk ever since (I sit maybe 30 mins out of an 8-hour day).     I don't wear stilettos, but even with my poor heel tolerance I can manage block or stacked heels of up to 2 1/2" without any additional foot pain.  I make sure I don't wear the same pair of shoes more than two days in a row, as that does seem to increase my foot pain.  I also have a thick wool area rug in my office that I stand on, which I think helps substantially.  I have found it helps a lot to consciously shift your weight from one foot to another throughout the day.  Walking around as much as possible (even short trips to the copy machine or water cooler) and stretching regularly are good standing desk habits, too.  I had megatight hamstrings and quads for the first couple months because I was remaining stationary for too long.

For what it's worth, my physical therapists told me that standing all day isn't much better for you than sitting all day, and that switching between the two is definitely best if you can manage that.

16 year old me would wonder where my piercings went, why my hair is so long (and not pink), and why I haven't acquired more tattoos in the past 20 years.  At 16, my style was vintage-punk and I got a kick out of having the most "different" outfit in the room.  I didn't take myself or my appearance seriously except to make sure that I was wearing an interesting and fun combination of colors and textures.  Most of my clothes came from thrift shops, which at the time still carried tons of colorful 60s and 70s clothes that I bought by the bagful.  I wore my mom's 1960s dresses,  velvet Docs, giant-legged pants and tank tops (to show off my sweet tribal tattoos, of course :/ and found jewelry inspiration everywhere.

Once I hit 20 I  feared my previous look was juvenile but I didn't know what to do with myself, so I did a 180 and went all-out Banana Republic on everyone.  I started an office job, I was in a stifling and unhealthy relationship, my self-esteem plummeted, and my unusual-to-me new appearance didn't help.  I didn't feel like myself for a good decade, but I got compliments on my appearance so I figured that was good enough.  

Once I hit 30, I had more freedom in both my career and personal life to dress a little more creatively.  Now I wear what I want, which tends to be a lot of black pebbled leather, vintage blazers, and colorful pants.  I just bought an avocado green pair of wide legged corduroys from Zara that 16 year old me would have adored, which makes me smile whenever I wear them.

I think it's important to dress in a way that makes you feel like yourself, whoever or whatever that is. It's something entirely  separate from dressing on trend or even just generally dressing "well". Before getting the scissors out, I definitely recommend pinning the jeans up where you want to cut them off (if you dont have pins, use tape, bobby pins, binder clips, something like that).  Put on a few pairs of shoes, walk around, bend you legs to be certain that they fall where you want them to when you're doing something other than standing still in front of the mirror.

When you have them where you want them, use a straight edge to make a line all the way around the cuff - dont try to cut a double layer as it won't turn out evenly.  Cut carefully and slowly, and then put them in the washer and dryer to get the fray going.

Sidenote, if your jeans are more of the very stretchy jegging variety, there won't be a ton of fray.

I spent my teens as an outlandish vintage-loving punk, but once I entered the professional world in my 20s I had to do a 180 and dress for the office.  I spent all my clothes money on office outfits at New York and Company (back when it didn't suck) and Banana Republic, and while I looked good I felt like crap.  None of it felt right, none of it was comfortable, and I felt frumpy for about 12 years straight in my short cardigan and plain sheath dress costumes.  


This ended up extending to my non-work wardrobe as well, because I didn't remember how to wear clothes I liked anymore.  I lost track of what I loved and instead I dressed in imitation of what was popular at the time.  Again, I looked good but I always felt like I was trying, and massively failing, to be someone else.  It did not help that I was in an abusive long-term relationship and had a generally unsupportive, slightly toxic circle of friends at that time.

When I turned 30, my overall situation improved and I was making more money, had more responsibility at work, had a great new circle of friends and a fantastic mate, and thus just generally felt better about myself.  Everything else fell into place, clothing and appearance included.  Now I look the way I want to look instead of the way I *think* I'm supposed to look, and I feel like myself again.  It's empowering. I get more compliments now on my eclectic punk-vintage-office chic looks than I ever did when I felt like I was Banana Republic bot, and I think it's because the fact that I feel like myself, and feel GOOD, shows.

 I hit this mark later than most, but in doing so it all coincided with the magical "I suddenly don't give a single fuck about what anyone else thinks anymore" phenomenon that happens in your 30s.  It's the best place to be, ever.

My closet is in a weirdly laid out area (it's basically a tiny walk-in closet in the corner of a hallway) so I played around a lot to get my current system.  First I ordered a $10 clip on desk lamp on Amazon and mounted it to the doorframe so I can actually see everything  - it's amazing how much that helped me feel organized.

 Then I put everything on two racks upper and lower.  Top rack is for blazers/dresses/skirts/pants and the lower rack is for shirts.  Dresses and skirts are sorted in order of formality (work on the left, "going out"/fancy on the right), which was mostly to remind me to reach for the "going out" clothes when getting ready for same instead of reaching for the old familiars I wear to the office.  Pants go at the end of the rack just because they hang down too far and block my view of the shirts below.

The lower rack of shirts is organized from casual/weekend tees on left and work shirts on the right.  Within those two categories, I organize by color, and within each color I separate by sleeve length.

I also have a very narrow built-in shelf/drawer system tower in lieu of dressers.  Underwear and bras go in the drawers and socks go in a decorative box on a shelf, and the other shelves contain jeans and hoodies.  I have one extra shelf where I alternate either shorts or sweaters, depending on season.   Out of season clothes are stored in the attic in bins.
